title: Do one-way functions imply public-key encryption in the standard model?
question: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme with negligible correctness error and security against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversaries? General constructions and security proofs may use the code of the one-way function; they need not be black-box.

source.title: Foundations of Cryptography, Lecture 10

why: This is the main unresolved boundary between the assumptions needed for private-key and public-key cryptography. It asks whether generic computational one-wayness already contains the structure needed to establish encrypted communication without a pre-shared secret.

title: Does P≠NP imply the existence of one-way functions?
question: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?

source.title: Mathematics and Computation

why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
question: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.

title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
question: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
